text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- According to a Nordic consumer survey, Denmark has the most expensive insurance rates in the region, especially for life insurance policies, with tariffs in some cases thrice the price in Sweden.

-- Shares in FC Brondby, which lost to Spain's Tenerife in an UEFA Cup soccer second leg quarter-final match on Tuesday, plunged almost 25 percent after the defeat, rallying again to 315 crowns, 22 crowns above the level the paper reached after the star Copenhagen team's first leg victory.

-- Plans by Danish tax minister Carsten Koch to substitute vehicle excise duties with green taxes based on the environmental friendliness of cars have hit trouble, with the opposition Liberal Party hostile to the idea.

--A new survey by the Danish Chamber of Commerce shows that for every three production jobs moved to eastern Europe from Denmark two new jobs are created in the business sector at home. Denmark is poised for a new boom in business with eastern Europe, but there is a dearth of qualified marketing and product development staff.

--Denmark, its troubled shipbuilding sector hit by competition and subsidies in competing countries, is set to oppose European Commission plans for massive 10 billion crown state subsidies for shipyards in Germany, Greece and Spain but seems likely to lose its fight. Denmark rejects EU claims that the aid package will not distort competition in the industry.

--The EU Commission is to look again into Denmark's ban on soft drinks and beer cans, maintaining that the country's deposit system on bottles violates the union's trading and competition rules. Danish environmental minister Svend Auken says he will fight to maintain Denmark's bottle deposit system which he considers is the best on environmental grounds but is willing to discuss a compromise with EU environmental commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard.

--Denmark invested 20 billion crowns overseas in 1996, while foreign companies invested only 10 billion crowns in Denmark, according to a Central Bank survey. The Danish Federation of Industry says the dramatic fall in foreign investment in Denmark comes as no surprise due to the poor business climate at home, high corporate taxes and the strong crown currency.
